correctness.rationale: The recurrence addition identity and a quadratic algebraic norm yield rigorous index and jump bounds. More directly, a seven-case split for coefficient a=2,3,4,5..9,10,11..19,>=20 excludes all unlisted decimal edges using monotonicity and explicit first jumps. Exact integer checker independently reproduces the graph for 299 coefficient values, crosschecks 4321 general-base finite searches, and verifies 6525 addition identities and 64815 norms. The universal classification does not rely on finite extrapolation.

originality.rationale: Primary full-text inspection shows Miller et al. (2022) treated decimal append walks only for the ordinary Fibonacci sequence; the earlier 2020 prime/square-free walking paper covers other sets. Crucially, Kominers (arXiv:2512.06446, 2025) proves general termination of bounded-digit Lucas walks (Theorem 4.2, explicitly including Pell) and is acknowledged as dominating the simple finiteness consequence; the accepted claim is narrowed to the exact all-coefficient decimal edge graph, which the inspected theorem does not determine. published-finding corpus queries for right-truncatable Pell/Lucas and digit concatenation graphs found no equivalent exact classification. Unindexed equivalent tables remain a risk.
residual_risks: Unindexed Horadam/Lucas digit-concatenation literature or unpublished notes could contain equivalent results.
The OEIS page is long; selected inspected content is insufficient to exclude every linked table across the whole database.
The general-base bound is sufficient, not optimal; its elementary form may have appeared as a standard lemma under different terminology.

A separately published exact classification under right truncatable Lucas or generalized Fibonacci terminology could still cover the graph; the strongest readily accessible general Lucas theorem does not.

value.rationale: The 2022 Fibonacci walk problem and 2025 general Lucas termination result make exact digit-extension behavior a natural invariant. The new theorem exhaustively determines every decimal edge across the entire infinite positive-integer coefficient family, locating two and only two exceptional three-vertex walks (coefficients 3 and 10); neither generic termination nor Fibonacci-only bounds provides that information. This is a complete, sharp parameter classification with structural explanation, not a finite ad-hoc slice. The supporting general-base norm estimate is not itself counted as new value.
